summary: Describes the OSPFv3 extensions required for Segment Routing with the MPLS data plane. It lets OSPFv3 routers advertise segments so end-to-end paths can be built from subpaths.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment Routing builds a path out of numbered steps called segments. For that to work, every router in the network has to say which segments it can handle, and OSPFv3 is the protocol that spreads that information inside an IPv6 network. RFC 8666 defines the extra fields OSPFv3 uses for that, so no separate label-signalling protocol is needed.

questions: what is segment routing in ospfv3
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers advertise Segment Routing identifiers so IPv6 networks can steer MPLS traffic along paths built from segments.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing needs the routers of an interior gateway protocol to advertise the segments they can forward on, so that paths can be built from a list of segments. Without those advertisements there is no way to send traffic along a chosen path.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8666 adds OSPFv3 sub-TLVs that carry a Prefix-SID, an Adjacency SID, a LAN Adjacency SID and a generic SID or label, plus a top-level TLV that advertises a SID for a whole range of prefixes at once. Each sub-TLV carries flags that say how the value should be used.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 can advertise and distribute the segments an MPLS data plane needs, with no LDP or RSVP-TE signalling involved. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8666 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019, and it has not been obsoleted. It covers Segment Routing with the MPLS data plane; the OSPFv3 extension for the IPv6 data plane is specified separately.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Segment Routing allows a flexible definition of end-to-end paths within IGP topologies by encoding paths as sequences of topological subpaths called segments. These segments are advertised by the link-state routing protocols, IS-IS and OSPF. Prefix segments represent an ECMP-aware shortest path to a prefix or a node, as per the state of the IGP topology. Adjacency segments represent a hop over a specific adjacency between two nodes in the IGP. A prefix segment is typically a multi-hop path, while an adjacency segment is in most cases a one-hop path.

The control plane of Segment Routing can be applied to both IPv6 and MPLS data planes, and it does not require any additional signalling other than IGP extensions. The IPv6 data plane is out of the scope of this specification, as the OSPFv3 extension for SR with the IPv6 data plane is to be specified in a separate document. When used in MPLS networks, Segment Routing paths do not require any LDP or RSVP-TE signalling, although SR can interoperate in the presence of Label Switched Paths established with RSVP or LDP.

This document describes the OSPFv3 extensions required for Segment Routing with the MPLS data plane. The Segment Routing architecture is described in RFC 8402, and Segment Routing use cases in RFC 7855.
sections.plainLanguage: With Segment Routing, a path is a list of numbers rather than a set of instructions to each router. Each number names a segment: either the normal shortest path to a place, or the direct link to one neighbour. The interior gateway protocol spreads the list of available numbers so that any router can build such a path.

sections.title: Segment Routing Identifiers
sections.content:
Segment Routing defines various types of Segment Identifiers: Prefix-SID, Adjacency SID, and LAN Adjacency SID.

The SID/Label sub-TLV appears in multiple TLVs or sub-TLVs defined later in the document. It is used to advertise the SID or label associated with a prefix or adjacency. It has a 16-bit Type field with the value 7, a 16-bit Length field, and a variable SID/Label field. The Length is 3 or 4 octets. If the length is set to 3, then the 20 rightmost bits represent a label; if the length is set to 4, then the value represents a 32-bit SID.

Segment Routing also requires some additional router capabilities to be advertised to other routers in the area. These capabilities are advertised in the OSPFv3 Router Information Opaque LSA defined in RFC 7770 and specified in RFC 8665.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of segment identifier: one for a prefix, one for a direct neighbour link, and one for a neighbour on a shared network. The smallest building block is a generic SID or label field, three or four octets long, that is carried inside the other structures.

sections.title: The OSPFv3 Extended Prefix Range TLV
sections.content:
In some cases it is useful to advertise attributes for a range of prefixes in a single advertisement. The SR Mapping Server, described in RFC 8661, is an example of where SIDs for multiple prefixes can be advertised. To optimize such an advertisement in the case of multiple prefixes from a contiguous address range, the OSPFv3 Extended Prefix Range TLV is defined.

It is a top-level TLV of the E-Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA, the E-Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA, the E-AS-External-LSA and the E-Type-7-LSA, all defined in RFC 8362. Multiple such TLVs may be advertised in each of those LSAs. The TLV has a Type field with the value 9, a variable Length in octets depending on the sub-TLVs, a Prefix Length field giving the length of the prefix in bits, an Address Family field, a Range Size field, a Flags field that is reserved and must be zero when sent, a Reserved field, a variable Address Prefix field, and variable Sub-TLVs.

The address family is 0 for IPv4 unicast and 1 for IPv6 unicast. The Range Size represents the number of prefixes covered by the advertisement, and must not exceed the number of prefixes that could be satisfied by the Prefix Length without including addresses from the IPv4 multicast address range 224.0.0.0/3, if the address family is IPv4 unicast, or addresses other than IPv6 unicast addresses, if the address family is IPv6 unicast. The range represents the contiguous set of prefixes with the same prefix length as specified by the Prefix Length field, and it starts with the prefix given in the Address Prefix field.

For IPv4 unicast, the prefix itself is encoded as a 32-bit value and the default route is a prefix of length 0. For IPv6 unicast the prefix is encoded as an even multiple of 32-bit words, padded with zeroed bits as necessary, consuming ((PrefixLength + 31) / 32) 32-bit words. If Extended Prefix Range TLVs advertising the exact same range appear in multiple LSAs of the same type from the same OSPFv3 router, the LSA with the numerically smallest Instance ID must be used and the later instances ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Advertising a SID for every prefix one at a time is wasteful when the prefixes are consecutive. This TLV covers a whole run of prefixes in one go: it names the first prefix, the prefix length, and how many prefixes follow. The prefix-SID inside it then means the first value in the run, with the next prefix taking the next value.

sections.title: The Prefix-SID Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Prefix-SID sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the Intra-Area Prefix TLV, the Inter-Area Prefix TLV, the External Prefix TLV and the OSPFv3 Extended Prefix Range TLV. It may appear more than once in the parent TLV. It has a Type field with the value 4, a Length of 7 or 8 octets depending on the V-Flag, a single-octet Flags field, a single-octet Algorithm field, a Reserved field, and a variable SID/Index/Label field.

Five flags are defined in the Flags field. The NP-Flag, no penultimate hop popping, means that if it is set the penultimate hop must not pop the Prefix-SID before delivering packets to the node that advertised it. The M-Flag, mapping server flag, means the SID was advertised by an SR Mapping Server. The E-Flag, explicit null flag, means that any upstream neighbour of the Prefix-SID originator must replace the Prefix-SID with the Explicit NULL label, 0 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6, before forwarding the packet. The V-Flag, value or index flag, says whether the Prefix-SID carries an absolute value or an index. The L-Flag, local or global flag, says whether the value or index has local or global significance. The remaining bits are reserved, must be zero when sent and are ignored when received.

The Algorithm field is a single octet identifying the algorithm the Prefix-SID is associated with, as defined in the IGP Algorithm Types registry. A router receiving a Prefix-SID from a remote node with an algorithm value that the remote node has not advertised in the SR-Algorithm TLV must ignore the Prefix-SID sub-TLV. The SID/Index/Label field depends on the V-Flag and L-Flag: with the V-Flag set to 0 and the L-Flag set to 0 it is a 4-octet index defining the offset in the SID or label space advertised by this router; with the V-Flag set to 1 and the L-Flag set to 1 it is a 3-octet local label where the 20 rightmost bits encode the label value. All other combinations are invalid, and any SID advertisement with an invalid setting must be ignored.

If an OSPFv3 router advertises multiple Prefix-SIDs for the same prefix, topology and algorithm, all of them must be ignored. When calculating the outgoing label for the prefix, the router must take into account the E, NP and M flags advertised by the next-hop router if that router advertised the SID for the prefix, regardless of whether that router contributes to the best path.

The NP-Flag must be set and the E-Flag must be clear for Prefix-SIDs allocated to prefixes propagated between areas by an ABR based on intra-area or inter-area reachability, unless the advertised prefix is directly attached to that ABR, and likewise for redistributed prefixes unless the redistributed prefix is directly attached to the advertising ASBR. If the NP-Flag is not set, any upstream neighbour of the Prefix-SID originator must pop the Prefix-SID, which is the penultimate hop-popping mechanism used in the MPLS data plane, and the received E-Flag is ignored. If the NP-Flag is set and the E-Flag is not, any upstream neighbour must keep the Prefix-SID on top of the stack, which is useful when the originator needs to stitch the incoming packet into a continuing MPLS LSP, at an ABR or an ASBR. If both flags are set, any upstream neighbour must replace the Prefix-SID with an Explicit NULL label, which is useful when the originator is the final destination and wants the packet with the original Traffic Class field. When the M-Flag is set, the NP-Flag and the E-Flag must be ignored on reception.
sections.plainLanguage: The Prefix-SID sub-TLV says which number stands for a prefix, and how that number should be treated. The flags decide what the routers before the endpoint do with it: pop it, keep it, or replace it with an explicit null. The algorithm byte says which path-computation the number belongs to, and the two scope flags say whether the number is absolute or an offset into a block of numbers.

sections.title: Adjacency Segment Identifiers
sections.content:
An Adjacency Segment Identifier represents a router adjacency in Segment Routing.

The Adj-SID sub-TLV is an optional sub-TLV of the Router-Link TLV and may appear multiple times in it. It has a Type field with the value 5, a Length of 7 or 8 octets depending on the V-Flag, a single-octet Flags field, a single-octet Weight field used for load-balancing purposes, a Reserved field, and a variable SID/Label/Index field.

Five flags are defined. The B-Flag, backup flag, means the Adj-SID refers to an adjacency eligible for protection, for example using IP Fast Reroute or MPLS Fast Reroute. The V-Flag is the value or index flag. The L-Flag is the local or global flag. The G-Flag, group flag, indicates that the Adj-SID refers to a group of adjacencies and may therefore be assigned to other adjacencies as well. The P-Flag, persistent flag, indicates that the Adj-SID is persistently allocated, so its value remains the same across a router restart or an interface flap. The remaining bits are reserved.

An SR-capable router may allocate an Adj-SID for each of its adjacencies and set the B-Flag when the adjacency is eligible for protection by a fast reroute mechanism. It may allocate more than one Adj-SID to an adjacency, and it may allocate the same Adj-SID to different adjacencies. When the P-Flag is not set the Adj-SID may be persistent; when the P-Flag is set it must be.

The LAN Adjacency SID is an optional sub-TLV of the Router-Link TLV, and it may appear multiple times there. It is used to advertise a SID or label for an adjacency to a non-Designated Router on a broadcast, Non-Broadcast Multi-Access or hybrid network. It has a Type field with the value 6, a Length of 11 or 12 octets depending on the V-Flag, the same Flags and Weight fields as the Adj-SID sub-TLV, a Reserved field, a Neighbor ID field holding the Router ID of the neighbour for which the LAN Adjacency SID is advertised, and a variable SID/Label/Index field.
sections.plainLanguage: An adjacency segment names one direct link to one neighbour, so a path can steer traffic over a link that the shortest path would not choose. The backup flag marks links that a fast reroute could use, the group flag marks a set of links that share one number, and the persistent flag says the number survives a restart.

sections.title: Elements of Procedure
sections.content:
Intra-area. An OSPFv3 router that supports Segment Routing may advertise Prefix-SIDs for any prefix to which it is advertising reachability, such as a loopback address. A Prefix-SID can also be advertised by SR Mapping Servers. A Mapping Server advertises Prefix-SIDs for remote prefixes that exist in the OSPFv3 routing domain, and multiple Mapping Servers can advertise Prefix-SIDs for the same prefix, in which case the same Prefix-SID must be advertised by all of them. The Mapping Server can use either area flooding scope or autonomous system flooding scope, choosing the E-Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA or the E-AS-External-LSA accordingly. When a Prefix-SID is advertised by the Mapping Server, indicated by the M-Flag, the route type implied by the LSA type is ignored and the Prefix-SID is bound to the corresponding prefix independent of the route type. Advertisement of the Prefix-SID by the Mapping Server does not itself contribute to the prefix reachability, so the NU-bit must be set in the PrefixOptions field of the LSA. A Mapping Server must use the Extended Prefix Range TLVs when advertising SIDs for prefixes, and prefixes of different route types can be combined in a single such TLV.

Inter-area. To support SR in a multiarea environment, OSPFv3 must propagate Prefix-SID information between areas. When an ABR advertises an Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA from an intra-area prefix to all its connected areas, it also includes the Prefix-SID sub-TLV. The ABR looks at its best path to the prefix in the source area, finds the advertising router associated with that best path, and uses the Prefix-SID that router advertised. If no Prefix-SID was advertised for the prefix in the source area by the router that contributes to the best path, the ABR uses the Prefix-SID advertised by any other router. When an ABR advertises an Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA from an inter-area route, the same procedure is used with the backbone area as the source.

External prefixes. AS-External-LSAs are flooded domain wide. When an ASBR that supports SR originates an E-AS-External-LSA, it should also include a Prefix-SID sub-TLV, with the value set to the SID reserved for that prefix. When a Not-So-Stubby Area ABR translates an E-NSSA-LSA into an E-AS-External-LSA, it should also advertise the Prefix-SID for the prefix, taking it from the router associated with its best path to that prefix if that router advertised one, and otherwise from any other router.

Advertisement of Adj-SID. An Adj-SID may be advertised for any adjacency on a point-to-point link that is in neighbour state 2-Way or higher. If the adjacency transitions from the FULL state, the Adj-SID for that adjacency may be removed from the area; if it transitions to a state lower than 2-Way, the Adj-SID advertisement must be withdrawn from the area. Broadcast, NBMA and hybrid networks in OSPFv3 are represented by a star topology where the DR is the central point, so routers on such a network advertise only their adjacency to the DR. Each router may advertise the Adj-SID for its adjacency to the DR, and SR-capable routers may also advertise a LAN Adjacency SID for other neighbours, such as the Backup Designated Router or a DR-OTHER, on that network.
sections.plainLanguage: A router may advertise a segment for any prefix it already advertises reachability for. An area border router copies the segment into the other areas, taking it from the router on its best path. A border router outside the autonomous system does the same for external prefixes. A special server may also advertise segments for prefixes it does not originate, in which case the segment is not a reachability advertisement.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The specification updates two existing OSPFv3 registries. In the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA TLVs registry, the value 9 is allocated to the OSPFv3 Extended Prefix Range TLV. In the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry, the value 4 is allocated to the Prefix-SID sub-TLV, 5 to the Adj-SID sub-TLV, 6 to the LAN Adj-SID sub-TLV, and 7 to the SID/Label sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Four sub-TLV numbers and one TLV number are reserved so that every implementation uses the same numbers for the same things.

sections.title: Error Handling and Security Considerations
sections.content:
For any new TLVs or sub-TLVs defined in the document, if the length is invalid, the LSA in which it is advertised is considered malformed and must be ignored. Errors should be logged subject to rate limiting.

With the OSPFv3 Segment Routing extensions defined here, OSPFv3 will now program the MPLS data plane. Previously, LDP or another label distribution mechanism was required to advertise MPLS labels and program that data plane. In general, the same types of attacks that can be carried out on the IP control plane can be carried out on the MPLS control plane, resulting in traffic being misrouted in the respective data planes. However, the latter can be more difficult to detect and isolate.

Existing security extensions, as described in RFC 5340 and RFC 8362, apply to these Segment Routing extensions. While OSPFv3 is under a single administrative domain, there can be deployments where potential attackers have access to one or more networks in the OSPFv3 routing domain, and in those deployments stronger authentication mechanisms, such as those specified in RFC 4552 or RFC 7166, should be used.

Implementations must ensure that malformed TLVs and sub-TLVs defined in the document are detected and that they do not provide a vulnerability for attackers to crash the OSPFv3 router or routing process. Reception of a malformed TLV or sub-TLV should be counted and/or logged for further analysis, and logging of malformed TLVs and sub-TLVs should be rate limited to prevent a denial-of-service attack from overloading the OSPFv3 control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Two points. First, a malformed field makes the whole advertisement unusable, so it is thrown away rather than acted on. Second, because these extensions now let OSPFv3 steer MPLS traffic, a spoofed advertisement can send packets down the wrong path, and that is harder to notice than a spoofed IP route, so the stronger OSPFv3 authentication modes are worth using.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: 7 or 8 octets, depending on the V-Flag.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: The NP, M, E, V and L flags.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: The algorithm the Prefix-SID is associated with.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Should be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception.

items.label: No-PHP
items.desc: The penultimate hop must not pop the Prefix-SID before delivering packets to the node that advertised it.

items.label: Mapping Server
items.desc: The SID was advertised by an SR Mapping Server.

items.label: Explicit Null
items.desc: Upstream neighbours replace the Prefix-SID with the Explicit NULL label, 0 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6.

items.label: Value or Index
items.desc: Set means the Prefix-SID carries an absolute value; clear means it carries an index.

items.label: Local or Global
items.desc: Set means the value has local significance; clear means it has global significance.

items.label: Backup
items.desc: The adjacency is eligible for protection, for example by IP or MPLS Fast Reroute.

items.label: Value or Index
items.desc: Set means the Adj-SID carries an absolute value; clear means it carries an index.

items.label: Local or Global
items.desc: Set means the value has local significance; clear means it has global significance.

items.label: Group
items.desc: The Adj-SID refers to a group of adjacencies and may be assigned to others as well.

items.label: Persistent
items.desc: The Adj-SID value stays the same across a router restart or an interface flap.

viz.caption: The OSPFv3 sub-TLVs this document registers
The three kinds of Segment Identifier

items.title: Prefix-SID
items.text: Stands for an ECMP-aware shortest path to a prefix or a node, following the state of the IGP topology. Usually a multi-hop path.

items.title: Adjacency SID
items.text: Stands for a hop over one specific adjacency between two routers. Usually a one-hop path.

items.title: LAN Adjacency SID
items.text: Stands for a SID or label for an adjacency to a non-Designated Router on a broadcast, NBMA or hybrid network.
